questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀² xy dy dx.
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀² xy dy = x·[y²/2]₀² = 2x. Outer: ∫₀¹ 2x dx = [x²]₀¹ = 1. A definite double integral is a pure number, so no x can survive.
why_wrong: Dropped the 1/2 in ∫y dy = y²/2, so the inner integral became 4x and ∫₀¹ 4x dx = 2.
Stopped after the inner integration. 2x still contains x, but a definite double integral must be a pure number.
Used 0 to 1 for y as well, which integrates over the unit square, not over 0 ≤ y ≤ 2.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ (x + y) dy dx, where the inner integral runs over y from 0 to x.
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀ˣ (x + y) dy = [xy + y²/2]₀ˣ = x² + x²/2 = 3x²/2. Outer: ∫₀¹ 3x²/2 dx = [x³/2]₀¹ = 1/2.
why_wrong: Stopped after the inner integral. 3x²/2 still contains x, so the outer integration over x is missing.
Dropped the 1/2 in ∫y dy, which makes the inner result 2x² and ∫₀¹ 2x² dx = 2/3.
Used y from 0 to 1 instead of 0 to x, which is the unit square: ∫₀¹ (x + 1/2) dx = 1.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ e^(x + y) dx dy.
questions.explain: e^(x + y) = eˣ·eʸ and both pairs of limits are constants, so the integral splits into a product: (∫₀¹ eˣ dx)(∫₀¹ eʸ dy) = (e − 1)(e − 1) = (e − 1)².
why_wrong: Treated x + y as a single variable t running from 0 to 2 and computed ∫₀² eᵗ dt = e² − 1. There are two independent integrations, not one.
Added the two single integrals, (e − 1) + (e − 1), instead of multiplying them.
Did only one of the two integrations.

questions.q: The region 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 3 is a rectangle. Which expression is ∫₀² ∫₀³ f(x, y) dy dx with the order of integration reversed?
questions.explain: For a rectangle every limit is a constant, so each variable keeps its own limits when the order is reversed: x still runs 0 to 2 and y still runs 0 to 3. So ∫₀² ∫₀³ f dy dx = ∫₀³ ∫₀² f dx dy, with dx now on the inside, paired with 0 to 2.
why_wrong: Swapped only the differentials. x now runs 0 to 3 and y runs 0 to 2, which is a different rectangle.
Reversing the order of integration does not change the sign. Only swapping the two limits of a single integral does that.
A double integral splits into a product only when f(x, y) = g(x)h(y). For a general f, the y-integral still depends on x.

questions.q: Which region is the iterated integral ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ f(x, y) dy dx taken over? (Inner: y from 0 to x. Outer: x from 0 to 1.)
questions.explain: For each x in [0, 1], y runs from the x-axis (y = 0) up to the line y = x. Those vertical strips fill the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0) and (1, 1), which lies below the diagonal y = x.
why_wrong: This is 0 ≤ x ≤ y ≤ 1, the part above y = x. The limits 0 ≤ y ≤ x put the region below that line.
The inner upper limit is x, not 1, so each strip stops at the line y = x.
Took the slanted edge to be x + y = 1. The edge here is y = x.

questions.q: In plane polar coordinates x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, the area element dx dy becomes which of these?
questions.explain: ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = (cos θ)(r cos θ) − (−r sin θ)(sin θ) = r(cos²θ + sin²θ) = r. Since r ≥ 0, dx dy = r dr dθ.
why_wrong: Dropped the Jacobian r. dx dy is never just dr dθ.
Borrowed the r² from the spherical element. In the plane the factor is r.
Used the reciprocal Jacobian ∂(r, θ)/∂(x, y) = 1/r instead of ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r.

questions.q: In spherical coordinates x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ (θ measured from the positive z-axis, φ the azimuthal angle), the volume element dx dy dz becomes which of these?
options: r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
r² sin φ dr dθ dφ
r sin θ dr dθ dφ
questions.explain: For these formulas the Jacobian ∂(x, y, z)/∂(r, θ, φ) is r² sin θ, and sin θ ≥ 0 for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, so dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ. You get the same result from a thin spherical box with sides dr, r dθ and r sin θ dφ.
why_wrong: Put the sine of the azimuthal angle φ in the element. The sine belongs to the polar angle θ, which is measured from the z-axis.
Kept only one factor of r, as in plane polars. The spherical Jacobian has r².
Dropped the Jacobian entirely.

questions.q: In spherical coordinates x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ, with φ running from 0 to 2π, what range of θ covers the whole sphere r ≤ a exactly once?
questions.explain: With z = r cos θ, θ is measured down from the positive z-axis: θ = 0 is the top of the sphere and θ = π is the bottom. So 0 ≤ θ ≤ π together with 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π reaches every point once, and sin θ ≥ 0 throughout.
why_wrong: The polar angle only has to swing from the positive z-axis to the negative z-axis. Running it 0 to 2π covers the sphere twice, and with sin θ in the element the volume integral comes out 0.
This covers only the upper hemisphere, where z = r cos θ ≥ 0.
This is the latitude convention. With z = r cos θ it gives cos θ ≥ 0, which is only the upper hemisphere.

questions.q: In plane polar coordinates x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, what is the equation of the circle x² + y² = 2x?
questions.explain: Substitute x² + y² = r² and x = r cos θ to get r² = 2r cos θ. Dividing by r gives r = 2 cos θ. The pole r = 0 already lies on this curve, at θ = π/2.
why_wrong: Substituted y where x belongs. r = 2 sin θ is the circle x² + y² = 2y.
Used the radius 1 of (x − 1)² + y² = 1, but r = constant describes only circles centred at the origin.
Replaced x by cos θ instead of r cos θ, which loses a factor of r on the right.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ (x + y + z) dx dy dz.
questions.explain: Over the unit cube, ∭ x dV = (∫₀¹ x dx)·1·1 = 1/2, and the same holds for y and z. The integrand is a sum, so the three contributions add: 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2.
why_wrong: Multiplied the three 1/2's together. The integrand is a sum, so the three contributions add.
Took each ∫₀¹ x dx as 1 instead of 1/2.
Integrated only the x term and lost the y and z terms.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀² ∫₀³ xyz dz dy dx.
questions.explain: The integrand is the product xyz and every limit is a constant, so the integral splits: (∫₀¹ x dx)(∫₀² y dy)(∫₀³ z dz) = (1/2)(2)(9/2) = 9/2.
why_wrong: Integrated 1 instead of xyz. 6 = 1·2·3 is just the volume of the box.
Dropped every 1/2 by taking ∫x dx as x², which gives 1·4·9 = 36.
Added the three single integrals, 1/2 + 2 + 9/2, instead of multiplying them.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀³ ∫₀^(2x) dy dx, the area of the triangle bounded by y = 0, y = 2x and x = 3.
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀^(2x) dy = 2x, the height of a vertical strip. Outer: ∫₀³ 2x dx = [x²]₀³ = 9. This matches (1/2)·base·height = (1/2)·3·6.
why_wrong: Took y from 0 to 6 for every x. That is the 3 × 6 rectangle, not the triangle under y = 2x.
Stopped after the inner integral and put x = 3 into 2x. That is only the height of the last strip.
Dropped the inner integral and integrated dx alone. 3 is only the length of the base.

questions.q: Evaluate the area integral ∬ dy dx in which y runs from x² up to x (inner) and x runs from 0 to 1 (outer).
questions.explain: Inner: ∫ dy from y = x² to y = x gives x − x². Outer: ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. This is the area between the line y = x and the parabola y = x².
why_wrong: Subtracted the wrong way round, x² − x. On [0, 1] the line y = x lies above y = x², so upper minus lower is x − x².
Added the two areas, 1/2 + 1/3, instead of subtracting them.
Used only the upper curve y = x, which is the area under the line, and ignored the lower boundary y = x².

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀ᵃ r dr dθ, where a > 0.
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀ᵃ r dr = a²/2. Outer: ∫₀^(2π) (a²/2) dθ = πa², the area of a disc of radius a. The r in r dr dθ is what makes the result an area.
why_wrong: Dropped the r in r dr dθ and integrated dr dθ. The result 2πa has the value of the circumference, not the area.
Stopped after the inner integral and never integrated over θ.
Dropped the 1/2 in ∫ r dr = r²/2.

questions.q: Reverse the order of integration in ∫₀¹ ∫ₓ¹ f(x, y) dy dx, where y runs from x to 1 (inner) and x runs from 0 to 1 (outer). Which limits are correct for the order dx dy?
options: x from 0 to y, then y from 0 to 1
x from y to 1, then y from 0 to 1
x from x to 1, then y from 0 to 1
x from 0 to 1, then y from 0 to 1
questions.explain: The limits describe 0 ≤ x ≤ y ≤ 1, the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1), above the line y = x. A horizontal strip at height y runs from the y-axis (x = 0) to the line x = y, and y takes every value from 0 to 1. So the reversed integral is ∫₀¹ ∫₀ʸ f(x, y) dx dy.
why_wrong: Swapped the symbols mechanically. x from y to 1 describes the triangle below y = x, not the given one above it.
Kept x in the limits of the x-integral, so the result cannot be a pure number. The limits have to be re-derived from the region.
Replaced the triangle by the whole unit square. Each strip must stop at the line x = y.

questions.q: An integral has y running from x² to x (inner) and x running from 0 to 1 (outer). Which limits describe the same region in the order dx dy?
options: x from y² to y, then y from 0 to 1
x from √y to y, then y from 0 to 1
x from y to √y, then y from 0 to 1
x from y to √y, then y from x² to x
questions.explain: The region is x² ≤ y ≤ x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. It lies between the line y = x and the parabola y = x², which meet at (0, 0) and (1, 1). A horizontal strip at height y starts on the line (x = y) and ends on the parabola (x = √y), and y ≤ √y on [0, 1]. So the reversed form is one integral: x from y to √y, then y from 0 to 1.
why_wrong: Swapped the symbols mechanically. The limits must come from solving y = x and y = x² for x.
Right curves, wrong order. For 0 < y < 1 we have y < √y, so the left edge is x = y. Running x from √y down to y gives the negative of the correct value.
Left x in the outer limits. After the inner integration, the outer limits must be the constants 0 and 1.

questions.q: In the order dx dy, the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), (1, 1) is covered by: x from y to 2 − y, then y from 0 to 1. How is the same region written in the order dy dx?
options: One integral: y from 0 to x, then x from 0 to 2
One integral: y from x to 2 − x, then x from 0 to 1
Two integrals: y from x to 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, plus y from 2 − x to 1 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2
Two integrals: y from 0 to x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, plus y from 0 to 2 − x for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2
questions.explain: A vertical strip at x starts at y = 0, but its top changes: it is the edge y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and the edge y = 2 − x for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2. Because the upper boundary switches formula at x = 1, the dy dx form has to be split: ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ f dy dx + ∫₁² ∫₀^(2 − x) f dy dx. The same triangle needs only one integral in the order dx dy.
why_wrong: Used the left edge y = x across the whole base. For 1 < x ≤ 2 the top is y = 2 − x, so this covers the wrong triangle, (0, 0), (2, 0), (2, 2).
Swapped x and y symbol by symbol. This describes the triangle (0, 0), (0, 2), (1, 1).
Took each strip from the slanted edge up to y = 1. That is the part of the rectangle outside the triangle.

questions.q: By changing the order of integration, evaluate I = ∫₀¹ ∫ e^(x²) dx dy, where the inner integral runs from x = y to x = 1 and the outer from y = 0 to y = 1.
questions.explain: The region is 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1, so in the order dy dx it becomes y from 0 to x, then x from 0 to 1. Then I = ∫₀¹ e^(x²)·(x − 0) dx = ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx. With u = x², du = 2x dx: I = [e^(x²)/2]₀¹ = (e − 1)/2.
why_wrong: Lost the 1/2 that comes from the substitution u = x², du = 2x dx.
Evaluated e^(x²)/2 only at x = 1 and forgot to subtract its value, 1/2, at x = 0.
Took the new inner strip as y from x down to 0, which flips the sign.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) ∫₀^(π/2) sin(x + y) dx dy.
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀^(π/2) sin(x + y) dx = [−cos(x + y)]₀^(π/2) = −cos(π/2 + y) + cos y = sin y + cos y. Outer: ∫₀^(π/2) (sin y + cos y) dy = 1 + 1 = 2.
why_wrong: Split sin(x + y) as sin x + sin y, which is false. That split gives π/2 + π/2 = π.
Treated sin(x + y) as sin x · sin y and multiplied the two integrals, 1·1.
Used +cos as the antiderivative of sin, which flips the sign of the inner result.

questions.q: Which of these double integrals can NOT be split, as written, into a product (∫ g(x) dx)·(∫ h(y) dy) in which f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) and each single integral keeps its own limits?
questions.explain: A double integral splits into a product only when both conditions hold: the integrand has the form g(x)h(y), and every limit is a constant (the region is a rectangle). In ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ xy dy dx the inner limit depends on x, so the y-integral cannot be pulled out by itself. e^(x + y) = eˣ·eʸ and 1/(xy) = (1/x)(1/y) both split, because their limits are constant.
why_wrong: This one does split. The limits are constant and x²y = x²·y, giving (∫₀¹ x² dx)(∫₀² y dy) = (1/3)(2) = 2/3.
This one does split. e^(x + y) = eˣ·eʸ and the limits are constant, giving (e² − 1)(e − 1).
This one does split. 1/(xy) = (1/x)(1/y) on a rectangle, giving (ln 2)(ln 3).

questions.q: Under the substitution x = u + v, y = u − v, the area element dx dy becomes which of these?
questions.explain: ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = (∂x/∂u)(∂y/∂v) − (∂x/∂v)(∂y/∂u) = (1)(−1) − (1)(1) = −2. The area element uses the modulus: dx dy = |−2| du dv = 2 du dv.
why_wrong: Used the signed determinant. The area element needs its absolute value, |−2| = 2.
Used ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y), which is the reciprocal direction. Rewriting in u and v needs ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v).
Forgot the Jacobian factor altogether.

questions.q: Using plane polar coordinates, evaluate ∬ (x² + y²) dx dy over the disc x² + y² ≤ 1.
questions.explain: Here x² + y² = r² and dx dy = r dr dθ, and the disc is 0 ≤ r ≤ 1, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. So I = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀¹ r²·r dr dθ = 2π·[r⁴/4]₀¹ = 2π·(1/4) = π/2.
why_wrong: Dropped the r in r dr dθ: ∫₀¹ r² dr = 1/3, and 2π·(1/3) = 2π/3.
Let θ run only from 0 to π, which covers just half the disc.
Forgot the 1/4 in ∫₀¹ r³ dr = r⁴/4.

questions.q: In each iterated integral below, the differentials are listed innermost first. Which one is set up incorrectly, so that its value could not be a pure number?
options: ∫₀² ∫₀^(2 − x) ∫₀^(2 − x − y) f dz dy dx
questions.explain: A limit may involve only variables whose integrals sit further out, and the outermost limits must be constants. In ∫₀¹ ∫₀ʸ ∫₀¹ f dz dy dx, the middle integral is over y but has y as its upper limit, its own variable. So y never disappears and the result is not a number.
why_wrong: Valid. The dz limits use x and y, the dy limit uses x, both are integrated further out, and the outer limits are constants.
Valid. x runs 0 to y, y runs 0 to z, z runs 0 to 1, so each limit uses only variables integrated further out.
Valid. This is the standard set-up for the tetrahedron under x + y + z = 2, and its outer limits are constants.

questions.q: Take x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ, with θ measured from the positive z-axis. Which of these does NOT give the volume 4πa³/3 of the sphere r ≤ a?
options: ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀^π ∫₀ᵃ r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
8 ∫₀^(π/2) ∫₀^(π/2) ∫₀ᵃ r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
2 ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀^(π/2) ∫₀ᵃ r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
∫₀^π ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀ᵃ r² sin θ dr dθ dφ
questions.explain: In this option the θ-integral (the middle one) runs from 0 to 2π, and ∫₀^(2π) sin θ dθ = [−cos θ]₀^(2π) = 0, so the whole integral is 0. The polar angle, measured from the z-axis, must run only from 0 to π. It is φ that goes all the way round, 0 to 2π.
why_wrong: Valid. This is the whole sphere: (a³/3)·[−cos θ]₀^π·2π = (a³/3)(2)(2π) = 4πa³/3.
Valid. This is 8 times the first-octant piece: 8·(a³/3)(1)(π/2) = 4πa³/3.
Valid. This is twice the upper hemisphere: 2·(a³/3)(1)(2π) = 4πa³/3.

questions.q: Find the area of the region enclosed between the parabolas y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
questions.explain: The curves meet where (x²/4)² = 4x, i.e. x⁴ = 64x, so at x = 0 and x = 4. Between those points y = 2√x lies above y = x²/4, so Area = ∫₀⁴ (2√x − x²/4) dx = 32/3 − 16/3 = 16/3.
why_wrong: Found only the area under the upper curve y = 2√x and forgot to subtract the area under y = x²/4.
Subtracted the wrong way round, x²/4 − 2√x. On 0 < x < 4 the upper curve is y = 2√x.
Added the areas under the two curves, 32/3 + 16/3, instead of subtracting them.

questions.q: The volume of the tetrahedron bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane x + y + z = 2 is ∫₀² ∫₀^(2 − x) ∫₀^(2 − x − y) dz dy dx. What is its value?
questions.explain: Inner: ∫₀^(2 − x − y) dz = 2 − x − y. Middle: ∫₀^(2 − x) (2 − x − y) dy = (2 − x)²/2. Outer: ∫₀² (2 − x)²/2 dx = (1/2)(8/3) = 4/3, which agrees with (1/3)·base·height = (1/3)·2·2.
why_wrong: Dropped the 1/2 in the middle integral, which gives (2 − x)² and ∫₀² (2 − x)² dx = 8/3.
Treated the solid as a prism of height 2 over the base triangle of area 2. The top actually slopes down to zero.
Used 0 to 2 for all three variables, which gives the whole cube, not the tetrahedron.

questions.q: A thin metal plate occupies the triangle x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 1 (lengths in metres). Its surface density is ρ(x, y) = x + y kg/m², and its mass is M = ∬ ρ dA over the plate. What is M?
questions.explain: Take y from 0 to 1 − x inside and x from 0 to 1 outside. Inner: ∫₀^(1 − x) (x + y) dy = x(1 − x) + (1 − x)²/2 = (1 − x²)/2. Outer: ∫₀¹ (1 − x²)/2 dx = (1/2)(1 − 1/3) = 1/3 kg.
why_wrong: This is the area of the triangle, so the density was dropped (ρ taken as 1). Forgetting the 1/2 in ∫ y dy = y²/2 also gives 1/2.
Integrated over the whole unit square 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 instead of the triangle: ∫₀¹ ∫₀¹ (x + y) dy dx = 1.
Stopped after the inner integral. A definite double integral is a number, so x must still be integrated from 0 to 1.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ e^(y/x) dy dx, where the inner integral runs over y from 0 to x.
questions.explain: In the inner integral x is a constant, so ∫ e^(y/x) dy = x·e^(y/x). Then ∫₀ˣ e^(y/x) dy = x(e¹ − e⁰) = x(e − 1). Outer: ∫₀¹ x(e − 1) dx = (e − 1)/2.
why_wrong: Wrote ∫ e^(y/x) dy = e^(y/x) and dropped the factor x that comes from integrating e^(y/x) with respect to y.
Forgot the lower limit. At y = 0 the value is e⁰ = 1, not 0, so the inner result is x(e − 1), not x·e.
Divided by x instead of multiplying (antiderivative written as e^(y/x)/x). That gives (e − 1)/x and a false divergence at x = 0.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀ʸ x²y dx dy, where the inner integral is in x from 0 to y and the outer is in y from 0 to 1.
questions.explain: The inner variable is x, so y is held constant: ∫₀ʸ x²y dx = y·y³/3 = y⁴/3. Then ∫₀¹ y⁴/3 dy = 1/15. The region is the triangle 0 ≤ x ≤ y ≤ 1, above the line y = x.
why_wrong: Integrated over the other triangle, 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1, by attaching the limit 0 to y to the wrong variable: ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ x²y dy dx = 1/10.
Ignored the variable upper limit and integrated over the whole unit square: (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6.
Dropped the 1/3 from ∫ x² dx = x³/3, leaving ∫₀¹ y⁴ dy = 1/5.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀² ∫₀² |x − y| dy dx.
questions.explain: |x − y| changes form on the line y = x, so split the square there. By symmetry the two triangles contribute equally: ∫₀² ∫₀ˣ (x − y) dy dx = ∫₀² x²/2 dx = 4/3. Total = 2·(4/3) = 8/3. An integrand that is never negative cannot give 0 or a negative value.
why_wrong: Split at y = x but used y − x where y < x and x − y where y > x. The signs are swapped, so every piece comes out negative.
Dropped the modulus and integrated x − y, so the two triangles cancel.
Computed only the triangle below y = x and forgot the equal contribution from the triangle above it.

questions.q: Change the order of integration in ∫₀² ∫ f(x, y) dy dx, where y runs from x²/2 to 4 − x (inner) and x from 0 to 2 (outer). Which gives the same region in the order dx dy?
options: x from 0 to √(2y) for 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, plus x from 0 to 4 − y for 2 ≤ y ≤ 4
x from √(2y) to 4 − y, then y from 0 to 4 (one integral)
x from 0 to 4 − y for 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, plus x from 0 to √(2y) for 2 ≤ y ≤ 4
x from 0 to √(2y), then y from 0 to 4 (one integral)
questions.explain: Sketch it. The region is bounded by x = 0, the parabola x² = 2y and the line x + y = 4, which meet at (2, 2), so its corners are (0, 0), (0, 4) and (2, 2). A horizontal strip starts at x = 0 and ends on the parabola x = √(2y) while y ≤ 2, and on the line x = 4 − y once y ≥ 2. The right wall changes at y = 2, so the reversed form needs two integrals.
why_wrong: This strip runs from the parabola to the line, which is outside the region. The left wall is x = 0, and in this order the region does not fit one integral.
Splitting at y = 2 is right, but the boundaries are on the wrong pieces. The parabola bounds the lower part and the line bounds the upper part.
Used only the parabola as the right wall. Above y = 2 the parabola lies outside the region, so the line x = 4 − y takes over.

questions.q: Reverse the order of integration in ∫₀¹ ∫ f(x, y) dy dx, where y runs from eˣ to e (inner) and x from 0 to 1 (outer). Which limits describe the same region in the order dx dy?
options: x from ln y to 1, then y from 1 to e
x from 0 to ln y, then y from 0 to e
x from 0 to ln y, then y from 1 to e
x from 0 to ln y, then y from 0 to 1
questions.explain: The region lies above y = eˣ and below y = e for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. It is a curved triangle with corners (0, 1), (0, e) and (1, e). Since eˣ ≥ 1 there, y runs from 1 to e. For a fixed y, a horizontal strip goes from x = 0 to the curve y = eˣ, i.e. x = ln y.
why_wrong: This strip runs from the curve across to x = 1, which is the region below y = eˣ, not above it.
y never drops below e⁰ = 1 in this region. For 0 < y < 1, ln y is negative and there is no strip.
Kept the old x-limits 0 and 1 as the y-limits instead of reading the y-range off the region.

questions.q: Evaluate I = ∫₀¹ ∫ x²e^(xy) dx dy, where x runs from y to 1 (inner) and y from 0 to 1 (outer), by first changing the order of integration.
questions.explain: The region is 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1, below the line y = x. Reversed, y runs from 0 to x and then x from 0 to 1. Inner: ∫₀ˣ x²e^(xy) dy = x²·[e^(xy)/x]₀ˣ = x(e^(x²) − 1). Outer: ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx − ∫₀¹ x dx = (e − 1)/2 − 1/2 = (e − 2)/2.
why_wrong: Swapped the limits mechanically to y from x to 1. That is the triangle above y = x, the wrong region.
Dropped the lower-limit term e⁰ = 1 in the inner integral, and with it the −∫₀¹ x dx = −1/2.
Lost the factor 1/2 in both ∫ x e^(x²) dx = e^(x²)/2 and ∫ x dx = x²/2.

questions.q: The sum ∫₀¹ ∫₀^(x²) f dy dx + ∫₁² ∫₀¹ f dy dx covers one connected region (dy is the inner integral in both). Which single integral in the order dx dy covers the same region?
options: x from 0 to √y, then y from 0 to 1
x from y² to 2, then y from 0 to 1
x from √y to 1, then y from 0 to 1
x from √y to 2, then y from 0 to 1
questions.explain: The first piece lies under y = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. The second is the square 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1. Together they form the region under y = x² up to x = 1 and under y = 1 from there to x = 2. For a fixed y between 0 and 1, a horizontal strip starts on the parabola x = √y and runs right to x = 2, so one integral is enough.
why_wrong: Took the strip on the wrong side of the parabola. 0 ≤ x ≤ √y is the region above y = x², which neither piece contains.
Inverted y = x² as x = y² by swapping symbols. Solving y = x² for x gives x = √y.
Covers only the first piece. The strip carries on through the square 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 to x = 2.

questions.q: In ∫₀² ∫ f dy dx, y runs from √(2x − x²) to √(2x) (inner) and x from 0 to 2 (outer). The region lies between the upper half of the circle (x − 1)² + y² = 1 and the parabola y² = 2x. When the order is reversed to dx dy, how many integrals are needed?
options: Two: split at y = 1, where the semicircle reaches its highest point
One: x from y²/2 to 2, then y from 0 to 2
Three: for 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 a horizontal line crosses the region in two separate pieces, one on each side of the semicircle, and 1 ≤ y ≤ 2 needs a third
Two: one integral left of the semicircle and one right of it, each with y from 0 to 2
questions.explain: For 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, a horizontal line enters at the parabola x = y²/2 and leaves at the left arc x = 1 − √(1 − y²). It skips the semicircle, then runs from the right arc x = 1 + √(1 − y²) to x = 2. That is two x-intervals, so two integrals. For 1 ≤ y ≤ 2 the circle is out of the way and x runs from y²/2 to 2, which gives a third integral.
why_wrong: Splitting at y = 1 is right, but below y = 1 each horizontal line meets the region in two separate intervals, so that band alone needs two integrals.
Ignores the semicircular hole. Points under the semicircle are not in the region, so for y < 1, x cannot run straight from the parabola to 2.
The circle only reaches y = 1, so 1 − √(1 − y²) is undefined for y > 1. The band 1 ≤ y ≤ 2 needs an integral of its own.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ ∫₀^∞ e^(−(x² + y²)) dx dy by changing to plane polar coordinates.
questions.explain: The region x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 is the first quadrant, so r runs from 0 to ∞ and θ from 0 to π/2, with dx dy = r dr dθ. The r-integral is ∫₀^∞ e^(−r²) r dr = [−e^(−r²)/2]₀^∞ = 1/2. So I = (π/2)·(1/2) = π/4.
why_wrong: Let θ run from 0 to 2π, which covers the whole plane rather than the first quadrant.
Dropped the 1/2 in ∫₀^∞ r e^(−r²) dr = 1/2.
Dropped the factor r from the area element (dx dy = dr dθ), leaving ∫₀^∞ e^(−r²) dr = √π/2.

questions.q: Change to polar coordinates and evaluate ∫₀ᵃ ∫ x/(x² + y²) dx dy, where x runs from y to a (inner) and y from 0 to a (outer), with a > 0.
questions.explain: The region is the triangle 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ a, between the x-axis and y = x and closed off by the line x = a. In polars θ runs from 0 to π/4, and r runs from 0 to the line x = a, i.e. r = a sec θ. The integrand becomes r cos θ/r² and dx dy = r dr dθ, so I = ∫₀^(π/4) ∫₀^(a sec θ) cos θ dr dθ = ∫₀^(π/4) a dθ = πa/4.
why_wrong: Let θ run over the whole first quadrant (0 to π/2). The line y = x stops the region at θ = π/4.
Took r from 0 to a, which is a circular arc. The outer edge is the straight line x = a, which is r = a sec θ.
Simplified x² + y² to r instead of r², so the integrand became cos θ instead of cos θ/r.

questions.q: R is the square |x + y| ≤ 1, |x − y| ≤ 1. Using the substitution u = x + y, v = x − y, evaluate ∬ (x + y)² dx dy over R.
questions.explain: Here u and v are given in terms of x and y, so ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (1)(−1) − (1)(1) = −2. The integral needs the other direction: |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| = 1/|−2| = 1/2, so dx dy = (1/2) du dv. R becomes −1 ≤ u ≤ 1, −1 ≤ v ≤ 1, and I = (1/2)·∫₋₁¹ u² du·∫₋₁¹ dv = (1/2)(2/3)(2) = 2/3.
why_wrong: Replaced dx dy by du dv with no Jacobian at all.
Used |∂(u, v)/∂(x, y)| = 2 as the scale factor. That Jacobian goes the wrong way; you need its reciprocal.
Used the signed Jacobian −1/2 without the modulus. The area scale factor is always an absolute value.

questions.q: Find the area of the first-quadrant region bounded by the curves xy = 1, xy = 2, y = x and y = 4x, using the substitution u = xy, v = y/x.
questions.explain: The region becomes the rectangle 1 ≤ u ≤ 2, 1 ≤ v ≤ 4. ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = (y)(1/x) − (x)(−y/x²) = 2y/x = 2v, so dx dy = du dv/(2v). Area = ∫₁² ∫₁⁴ 1/(2v) dv du = (1/2) ln 4 = ln 2.
why_wrong: Took the area of the u–v rectangle, 1 × 3, with no Jacobian.
Got ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) = v by dropping one of its two equal terms y/x, which gives ∫∫ dv/v = ln 4.
Multiplied by 2v instead of dividing by it. That uses ∂(u, v)/∂(x, y) where ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) = 1/(2v) is needed: ∫₁² ∫₁⁴ 2v dv du = 15.

questions.q: Using spherical coordinates x = r sin θ cos φ, y = r sin θ sin φ, z = r cos θ (θ measured from the positive z-axis), evaluate ∭ (x² + y² + z²) dV over the ball x² + y² + z² ≤ 1.
questions.explain: The integrand is r², and dV = r² sin θ dr dθ dφ with r from 0 to 1, θ from 0 to π and φ from 0 to 2π. I = ∫₀¹ r⁴ dr · ∫₀^π sin θ dθ · ∫₀^(2π) dφ = (1/5)(2)(2π) = 4π/5.
why_wrong: Dropped r² from the volume element, leaving ∫₀¹ r² dr = 1/3. That is just the volume of the ball, not the requested integral.
Dropped sin θ from the volume element, so ∫₀^π dθ = π replaced ∫₀^π sin θ dθ = 2.
Let θ run from 0 to 2π. θ is measured from the z-axis and only runs from 0 to π, and ∫₀^(2π) sin θ dθ = 0.

questions.q: A solid tetrahedron is bounded by the coordinate planes and the plane x + y + z = 1 (lengths in metres). Its density is ρ = x kg/m³, so its mass is ∭ x dV over the solid. What is the mass?
questions.explain: Limits: z from 0 to 1 − x − y, y from 0 to 1 − x, x from 0 to 1. ∫₀^(1 − x − y) x dz = x(1 − x − y). ∫₀^(1 − x) x(1 − x − y) dy = x(1 − x)²/2. ∫₀¹ x(1 − x)²/2 dx = (1/2)(1/12) = 1/24 kg.
why_wrong: This is the volume of the tetrahedron, so the density x was dropped.
Dropped the 1/2 in ∫₀^(1 − x) (1 − x − y) dy = (1 − x)²/2.
Integrated over the unit cube 0 ≤ x, y, z ≤ 1 instead of the tetrahedron.

questions.q: Using cylindrical coordinates (x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z), evaluate ∭ √(x² + y²) dV over the solid bounded below by the cone z = √(x² + y²) and above by the plane z = 1.
questions.explain: The integrand is r and dV = r dr dθ dz. The solid lies above the cone, so z runs from r to 1, with r from 0 to 1 and θ from 0 to 2π. I = ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀¹ ∫ᵣ¹ r·r dz dr dθ = 2π ∫₀¹ r²(1 − r) dr = 2π(1/3 − 1/4) = π/6.
why_wrong: Let θ run only from 0 to π, which covers half the solid.
Dropped the r in dV = r dr dθ dz, giving 2π ∫₀¹ r(1 − r) dr = π/3.
Took z from 0 to r. That is the region under the cone, not the solid between the cone and the plane.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ ∫₀^(√(1 − x²)) ∫₀^(√(1 − x² − y²)) xyz dz dy dx.
questions.explain: The region is the part of the unit ball in the first octant. Inner: ∫ z dz from 0 to √(1 − x² − y²) = (1 − x² − y²)/2. Over the quarter disc in polars, with xy = r² cos θ sin θ and dA = r dr dθ: (1/2) ∫₀^(π/2) cos θ sin θ dθ · ∫₀¹ r³(1 − r²) dr = (1/2)(1/2)(1/4 − 1/6) = 1/48.
why_wrong: Replaced every curved upper limit by 1 and integrated over the unit cube: (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Dropped the 1/2 from ∫ z dz = z²/2.
Dropped the factor r when switching the xy-integral to polars, giving (1/4) ∫₀¹ r²(1 − r²) dr = 1/30.

questions.q: Find the volume V = ∭ dV of the solid bounded below by the paraboloid z = x² + y² and above by the plane z = 2y.
questions.explain: The surfaces meet where x² + y² = 2y, the circle x² + (y − 1)² = 1, which is r = 2 sin θ in polars. The range 0 ≤ θ ≤ π traces it once. V = ∫₀^π ∫₀^(2 sin θ) (2r sin θ − r²) r dr dθ = ∫₀^π (4/3) sin⁴θ dθ = (4/3)(3π/8) = π/2. As a check, in polars centred at (0, 1) the height is 1 − s², and 2π ∫₀¹ (1 − s²) s ds = π/2.
why_wrong: Let θ run from 0 to 2π. r = 2 sin θ is negative for π < θ < 2π, and running θ over that range counts the disc a second time.
Dropped the r in dA = r dr dθ, giving (4/3) ∫₀^π sin³θ dθ = 16/9.
Integrated only the top surface, ∬ 2y dA = 2π, and forgot to subtract the paraboloid underneath.

questions.q: Using A = ∬ r dr dθ, find the area enclosed by the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ), where a > 0.
questions.explain: r runs from 0 to a(1 + cos θ) and θ from 0 to 2π. A = ∫₀^(2π) a²(1 + cos θ)²/2 dθ = (a²/2) ∫₀^(2π) (1 + 2 cos θ + cos²θ) dθ = (a²/2)(2π + 0 + π) = 3πa²/2.
why_wrong: Dropped the r from the area element. The result is a length, not an area.
Let θ run only from 0 to π, which covers only the half above the x-axis.
Dropped the 1/2 from ∫ r dr = r²/2.

questions.q: A vertical cylindrical tank x² + y² ≤ 9 (in metres) stands on the floor z = 0. It is closed by a slanted lid lying in the plane y + z = 5. What volume does the tank enclose between the floor and the lid?
questions.explain: The height above the point (x, y) is 5 − y, so V = ∬ (5 − y) dA over the disc r ≤ 3. In polars, ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀³ (5 − r sin θ) r dr dθ = 5·9π − 9·∫₀^(2π) sin θ dθ = 45π − 0 = 45π m³. The tilt adds as much height where y < 0 as it removes where y > 0.
why_wrong: Dropped the r from dA = r dr dθ: ∫₀^(2π) ∫₀³ 5 dr dθ = 30π.
Worked out the half-disc y ≥ 0 and doubled it. The lid is not symmetric about y = 0, so the y-term does not double. Over the full disc it cancels.
Used the greatest height, 8 m at y = −3, everywhere instead of integrating the varying height.

questions.q: Find the area of the region that lies inside the circle r = 2 cos θ and outside the circle r = 1.
questions.explain: The circles meet where 2 cos θ = 1, i.e. θ = ±π/3, and only between these angles is 2 cos θ ≥ 1. A = ∫ from −π/3 to π/3 of ∫₁^(2 cos θ) r dr dθ = (1/2) ∫ (4 cos²θ − 1) dθ = ∫₀^(π/3) (1 + 2 cos 2θ) dθ = π/3 + √3/2.
why_wrong: Dropped the 1/2 from ∫ r dr = r²/2.
Let θ run over −π/2 to π/2, the full range of r = 2 cos θ. Where |θ| > π/3 the unit circle lies outside r = 2 cos θ, so those parts subtract.
Subtracted the two full circle areas (π − π). The unit circle is not inside r = 2 cos θ, so the areas do not simply subtract.

questions.q: Find the area of the region bounded by the curve y = √x, the line y = 2 − x and the x-axis.
questions.explain: The curves meet at (1, 1), so the region has corners (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 0). In the order dx dy it is one integral: for 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, x runs from y² to 2 − y, so A = ∫₀¹ (2 − y − y²) dy = 2 − 1/2 − 1/3 = 7/6. In the order dy dx the top boundary changes at x = 1: ∫₀¹ √x dx + ∫₁² (2 − x) dx = 2/3 + 1/2 = 7/6.
why_wrong: This is the region between the two curves and the y-axis: ∫₀¹ (2 − x − √x) dx = 5/6.
Integrated only under y = √x from 0 to 1 and forgot the triangle under the line from x = 1 to 2.
Integrated √x all the way from 0 to 2 without switching to the line at x = 1.
